name: Dar Foto Festival
funding: Founded by Andrew Munuwa with Valentin Rudloff.
watch: Launched in 2023. The 2025 edition showed 15 artists from Congo, Sudan, Kenya and Tanzania in Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar (Musée Magazine, February 2025).
records_note: The About page names founder Andrew Munuwa and producer Tanzania Foto Collective Company Limited.
affiliations_note: Held its 2025 Coexistence exhibition at DARCH in the Old Boma building.

overview: Annual photography festival in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, with exhibitions, portfolio reviews, street and documentary photo walks, and conversations with professionals (PH Museum).

Founded by the Tanzanian photographer Andrew Stephen Munuwa, its Creative Director, with co-founder Valentin Rudloff of Germany (PH Museum; The Citizen; Humboldt Forum). Sources give different founding years: 2020 (Humboldt Forum), 2021 (PH Museum) and 2023 (The Citizen).
Munuwa is an independent photographer and curator from Dar es Salaam whose work focuses on everyday urban life in African cities (Humboldt Forum).

2024 edition (the second, per The Citizen): 2 February to 8 March 2024 at the Old Boma building in Posta, Dar es Salaam, with theme "People, Economy, Change", 12 Tanzanian artists, photo walks, panel discussions and mentorship. More than 800 visitors. A follow-up exhibition at the Emerson Art Gallery in Stone Town, Zanzibar, 21 June to 21 July 2024 (The Citizen, Ramadhani Ismail, 15 June 2024).
2025 edition: "Coexistence", 31 January to 1 March 2025 in Dar es Salaam and Stone Town (PH Museum).
The festival also staged a pop-up presentation on coexistence at the Humboldt Forum in Berlin, as part of its "Histories of Tanzania" exhibition (Humboldt Forum).
details.funding_verdict: Dar Foto Festival: founder-led: Andrew Munuwa and Valentin Rudloff
funding: Andrew Munuwa founded the festival and is its Creative Director (Humboldt Forum); the Humboldt Forum hosted the Berlin pop-up presentation.
Kedmon Mapana, Executive Secretary of BASATA, Tanzania's National Arts Council, said at the 2024 opening that "BASATA is keen to support the Dar Foto Festival in the coming years" (The Citizen).
details.bottom_line: Dar Foto Festival was founded by Andrew Munuwa and Valentin Rudloff, and Munuwa is its Creative Director. BASATA's Executive Secretary said in 2024 that the council is keen to support it.

name: Bangkok Kunsthalle
funding: Her husband Soopakij chairs CP Group, Thailand's largest private company.
watch: Activists from artn't staged a protest inside, in shirts reading 'world class exploitation'. CP Group's CP Foods faced 2014 slavery claims in its prawn-feed chain.
why_flagged: Opened January 2024 by philanthropist Marisa Chearavanont through her Khao Yai Art; no sponsors are named. She is married to Soopakij Chearavanont, chairman of CP Group.
records_note: No annual reports or accounts; the Team page names six individual donors without a date.
affiliations_note: Presented together with its sister site Khao Yai Art Forest, both founded by Marisa Chearavanont.

overview: Art centre at 599 Soi Phantha Chit (Pantachit Alley), Pom Prap Sattru Phai, in Bangkok's Yaowarat (Chinatown) district.
Founded by the art patron Marisa Chearavanont through her organisation Khao Yai Art. Opened in January 2024 with Michel Auder's "Nine Plus Five" (12 January to 11 February 2024).

Occupies the former headquarters of the printing house Thai Watana Panich: three connected buildings, the oldest over seven decades old, abandoned after a fire damaged the upper floors (ArtAsiaPacific; Wikipedia gives 2001 for the fire).
The brutalist complex covers nearly 65,000 square feet. In 2024 only the ground floor was in use, with plans to expand upward (Wikipedia; Art Basel).

Led by director and curator Stefano Rabolli Pansera, formerly director of Hauser & Wirth St. Moritz. It expects about four shows a year (Time Out Bangkok), has hosted artist residencies (Art Basel), and is the urban counterpart of Khao Yai Art Forest, about 150 km east of Bangkok.
Open Wednesday to Sunday 2pm to 8pm, closed Monday and Tuesday. Entry free (Time Out Bangkok).
details.funding_verdict: Bangkok Kunsthalle: private: the founder's philanthropy, from the Chearavanont family of CP Group
funding: Marisa Chearavanont is married to Soopakij Chearavanont, chairman of the Charoen Pokphand (CP) Group, which ArtReview calls Thailand's largest agribusiness (ArtAsiaPacific; ArtReview).
The art press describes the project as philanthropic; no source found gives an amount, a budget or a separate foundation's accounts.

red_flags.heading: Protest by artn't at the opening show
points: During Korakrit Arunanondchai's "nostalgia for unity" in 2024, two people from the Chiang Mai collective artn't appeared in the show in T-shirts reading "WORLD CLASS ARTIST, WORLD CLASS GALLERY, WORLD CLASS CORPORATION, WORLD CLASS EXPLOITATION" and "THIS COUNTRY IS YOUR GALLERY FOR EXHIBITING THE ART OF MONOPOLY" (ArtReview).
A member told ArtReview "the origins of art funding deserve critical examination."

A 2015 US lawsuit against Costco alleged that its prawns came from CP Foods, part of CP Group, and other suppliers that fed them fishmeal from slave-crewed boats, following a 2014 Guardian investigation (Taipei Times, from The Guardian); a US court dismissed the lawsuit against Costco and CP Foods, and CP Foods said it does not own the fishing vessels referenced (Wikipedia).

not_related: the Bangkok Art and Culture Centre (BACC), the city-backed centre in Pathum Wan whose 2025 censorship under Chinese embassy pressure has nothing to do with the Kunsthalle.

press.overall: One critical piece; other coverage is admiring features on the founder and director.

items.title: Pearamon Tulavardhana, "Will the New Bangkok Kunsthalle Fire up the Art Scene?" (2024)
points: "Philanthropy is crucial in a country where government funding for the arts is limited," but "concerns must be raised when an act of philanthropy may end up doing something else entirely."
Asks whether the space can start "critical conversations about the issues of exploitation and environment" around it, and notes rising rents in Chinatown and its disconnect from the neighbourhood.
Links the show's smoke to real haze from burning by contract corn farmers, without naming CP Group.

items.title: Nick Hackworth, "Can a kunsthalle turn Bangkok into Southeast Asia's premier art hub?" (2024)
points: Not criticism: an admiring feature that does not mention CP Group.

details.bottom_line: The money is the founder's own, and behind it sits the Chearavanont family's CP Group fortune; nothing is published on amounts or structure. The weak points are the undisclosed amounts and the CP Group connection, which artn't targeted at the opening show. Worth watching: whether Khao Yai Art publishes accounts or names funders.

name: Jim Thompson Art Center
funding: Run by the James H.W. Thompson Foundation, which says it relies entirely on its own funding.
watch: The foundation also supervises the Jim Thompson House Museum.
records_note: The art centre publishes nothing itself; its parent foundation lists seven trustees, says it funds itself.
affiliations_note: Run by the James H.W. Thompson Foundation, which also operates the Jim Thompson House Museum; the two sell a combined ticket.

overview: Contemporary art centre at No. 6 Soi Kasemsan 2, Rama 1 Road, Bangkok, about a 3-minute walk from the National Stadium BTS station (exit 1) and beside the Jim Thompson House Museum (Jim Thompson Art Center).

Run by the James H.W. Thompson Foundation, which was legally established in 1975 and also operates the Jim Thompson House Museum. The centre reopened on 27 November 2021 after about three years of construction on a new building and renovation of the house museum (ArtAsiaPacific, Pamela Wong, 29 November 2021; James H.W. Thompson Foundation).

Named for Jim Thompson, the American who founded the Thai Silk Company in 1951 and disappeared in Malaysia's Cameron Highlands on 27 March 1967. His nephew Henry B. Thompson III inherited the estate and donated the house and antiques to the foundation (James H.W. Thompson Foundation).

Building: a four-storey structure of about 3,000 square metres designed by the Bangkok studio Design Qua (ArtAsiaPacific). ArchDaily gives 3,800 square metres, lists steel, concrete and brick, and says the site was an outdoor car park serving the house museum, with an L-shaped new structure and an existing building forming a courtyard.
On site: two exhibition galleries, a rooftop space, a library, a cafe and a museum shop (ArtAsiaPacific).
Visiting: open every day 10am to 6pm. Admission 50 baht for the art centre alone, 250 baht with the Jim Thompson House Museum. Members and children under 10 enter free (Jim Thompson Art Center).
details.funding_verdict: Jim Thompson Art Center: self-funded by its foundation: stated by the foundation
funding: The James H.W. Thompson Foundation says it is a non-profit that "relies entirely on its own funding to carry out its activities". This is stated by the foundation; no source opened shows where that money comes from.

The foundation states its board has seven members and lists six current trustees: Vudthi Nathamethikul, Pinaree Sanpitak, Pawapun Bunnag Booth, Punthumadee Katawandee, Rachaporn Choochuey and Devid Teh.

press.overall: Coverage found is reporting on the 2021 reopening and listings.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the centre is stated by its foundation to be its own, with no named outside funder, so it cannot be traced further. The weak points are that the source of the foundation's income, its accounts and its seventh trustee are not published. Worth watching: whether the foundation publishes accounts that show how far house-museum admission pays for the art centre.

name: Chora Museum (Kariye)
funding: The pages read did not state funders. Bianet said a 1948 restoration was sponsored by the Byzantine Institute of America and Dumbarton Oaks.
watch: A Byzantine church made a mosque in 1511, a museum by a 1945 cabinet decree, and opened to worship again as a mosque on 21 August 2020 after the Council of State ruled on 11 November 2019 that its museum use was contrary to law (Bianet).
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: A former Byzantine monastery church outside the old walls of Constantinople, now the Kariye Mosque (Bianet).
Built as a monastery in 534, most of the present building dates from 1077 to 1081; mosque from 1511 for 434 years, museum by a 1945 decree and open to the public in 1958 (Bianet).
What is there: mosaics and frescoes, covered with plaster when it was a mosque and damaged by earthquakes; the page did not describe their subjects (Bianet).
Archive: none described in the page read.
details.funding_verdict: Chora: state, run as a mosque since 2020; the 1948 restoration was foreign-sponsored.
funding: The Byzantine Institute of America and Dumbarton Oaks sponsored a restoration programme in 1948 (Bianet).
No current funding figures found in the page read.

red_flags.heading: Reconversion
points: On 11 November 2019 the Council of State ruled that assigning the building to the Ministry of National Education as a museum and warehouse was contrary to law; a Presidential Decree opening it to worship was published in the Official Gazette on 21 August 2020 (Bianet).
In 2005 an association filed a lawsuit challenging its museum status (Bianet).

details.bottom_line: Public funding and decisions; the contested point is the 2020 conversion. No other money found.

name: Istanbul Archaeology Museums
funding: The pages read did not state cost or funders. Hürriyet Daily News (30 September 2019) said the renovation took nearly eight years and was announced by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, with Deputy Minister Nadir Alpaslan opening the renovated building on 27 September 2019.
watch: A Ministry of Culture and Tourism museum complex whose main building reopened on 27 September 2019 after nearly eight years of restoration, with seven exhibition halls and a store. The other two buildings were to open in 2020.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: A museum complex of three structures in Istanbul (Hürriyet Daily News, 30 September 2019).
The renovated section, halls 8 to 15, opened on 27 September 2019; the other two buildings were set to open in 2020 (Hürriyet Daily News, 30 September 2019).
What is there: seven exhibition halls and a museum store in the renovated part; no object count was given (Hürriyet Daily News, 30 September 2019).
Archive: the pages read did not describe an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Istanbul Archaeology Museums: state, Ministry of Culture and Tourism; no amounts found.
funding: The Ministry of Culture and Tourism issued the reopening statement (Hürriyet Daily News, 30 September 2019).
No reporting found, in the pages read, of the cost or funder of the renovation.
details.bottom_line: State-run; the pages read give no cost.

name: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations
funding: Run by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism; Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy inspected the renovation (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 July 2026). The article gave no cost or funding.
watch: A Ministry museum in the 15th-century Mahmut Paşa Bedesteni and Kurşunlu Han, which unveiled a renewed display of 288 newly shown artifacts in July 2026 after works begun in May 2026.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: A museum in two Ottoman buildings in Ankara, Mahmut Paşa Bedesteni and Kurşunlu Han (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 July 2026).
Converted into a museum in the early years of the Republic under Atatürk (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 July 2026).

What is there: 288 artifacts shown for the first time, a Göbeklitepe cult reconstruction, a Cybele statue and objects recovered from trafficking or repatriated from abroad (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 July 2026). No total was given.
Archive: none described.
details.funding_verdict: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations: state; no amounts found.
funding: Renovation launched May 2026; the article gave no cost (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 July 2026).
Further phases will update the Ankara and Classical Period sections and add basement galleries (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 July 2026).
details.bottom_line: A ministry-run archaeological museum; no controversy or amounts in the page read.

name: Rahmi M. Koç Museum
funding: Run by the Rahmi M. Koç Museology and Cultural Foundation, which acquired and restored the buildings; Rahmi M. Koç chaired its trustees (Koç Holding page). The page did not state how the museums are funded.
watch: A museum of industrial and transport history on the Golden Horn, opened in 1994 by a foundation chaired by Rahmi M. Koç, mostly from his private collection. The Koç Holding page lists further sites in Ankara and Ayvalık.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: Two sites on the Golden Horn, the Lengerhane Building and the Hasköy Dockyard, covering 27,000 square metres (Koç Holding).
Opened to visitors in 1994 by the Rahmi M. Koç Museology and Cultural Foundation (Koç Holding).

What is there: thousands of objects, mostly from Rahmi M. Koç's private collection, plus donations and loans (Koç Holding). The foundation also runs Çengelhan and Safranhan in Ankara and a museum in the Taksiyarhis Church in Ayvalık.
Archive: the Sevim and Necdet H. Kent Library in Ayvalık, with more than 1,300 books donated by Muhtar Kent (Koç Holding).
details.funding_verdict: Rahmi M. Koç Museum: private family foundation; the page did not state the budget.
funding: Rahmi M. Koç Museology and Cultural Foundation acquired and restored the buildings; Rahmi M. Koç chaired its Board of Trustees (Koç Holding).
The page sits in Koç Holding's sustainability section; no amounts.
details.bottom_line: The money is the Koç family's through its foundation; the page read gives no amounts and no controversy.

name: Zeugma Mosaic Museum
funding: The page read did not state funders. Hürriyet Daily News (23 April 2023) did not mention the Packard Humanities Institute or any other funder.
watch: A Ministry-run mosaic museum, closed 74 days after the 6 February 2023 earthquakes without damage and reopened in April 2023. Its display holds 2,500 square metres of mosaics, including the Gypsy Girl, and 12 pieces returned from the US in 2018.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: A museum of mosaics from Zeugma on the Euphrates, in Gaziantep (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 April 2023).
The page read did not give an opening year.

What is there: mosaics over 2,500 square metres including the Gypsy Girl and a Statue of Mars, Roman statues, columns and fountains, and 12 pieces returned from the US in 2018 (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 April 2023).
Archive: none described.
details.funding_verdict: Zeugma Mosaic Museum: state; the page read did not state funders.
funding: Ministry deputy general manager Yahya Coşkun said museums in the region will keep reopening (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 April 2023).
No reporting found, in the pages read, of the funder of the building or of budget.

red_flags.heading: February 2023 earthquake
points: Gaziantep museum director Özgür Çomak said the museum was shut as a precaution and had no cracks: 'we didn't lose a single one' of the mosaics; it reopened after 74 days (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 April 2023).

details.bottom_line: A state museum with no funding figures in the page read. No controversy found.

name: Dubai Opera
funding: The page read names Emaar as master developer and does not state who funds or owns the opera.
watch: A 2,000-seat venue in the Opera District, Downtown Dubai, built by master developer Emaar; Emaar chairman Mohammad Alabbar called it a tribute to the city, and Jasper Hope is its chief executive.
records_note: No accounts were found in the pages read.

overview: A multi-format venue of over 35,500 sq m built-up area in the Opera District, Downtown Dubai, near the Burj Khalifa (Gulf News).

Emaar is named as master developer; Mohammad Alabbar, chairman of Emaar Properties, called it a tribute to our city, and Jasper Hope is chief executive (Gulf News). The page read does not give the opening date.

What is there: a main hall of 2,000 seats that switches between theatre, concert and flat floor formats, a proscenium theatre, an acoustic concert hall and a 2,000 sq m event space; programme of opera, ballet, classical, musicals, Arab and world music, comedy, film, family shows and rock, pop and jazz concerts (Gulf News).
Archive: the page read describes none.
details.funding_verdict: Dubai Opera: developer Emaar named; funding and ownership not stated in the page read
funding: Emaar is described as master developer (Gulf News).
No reporting found, in the page read, of the cost, the owner, subsidies or sponsors.
details.bottom_line: The page read names Emaar as developer and nothing on who pays for operations. Ownership, subsidy and sponsors remain to be established.
details.website: https://www.dubaiopera.com (not opened; the site returned an access-denied error)

name: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi
funding: Owned by Abu Dhabi's state-owned Tourism Development and Investment Company; the Guggenheim Foundation runs the programme. The Department of Culture and Tourism set the opening for 11 December 2026.
watch: Gulf Labor Coalition has campaigned since 2011, with an artist boycott and New York Guggenheim protests in 2014 and 2015.
why_flagged: Owned by Abu Dhabi's state-owned Tourism Development and Investment Company; the Guggenheim Foundation runs the programme. The Department of Culture and Tourism set the opening for 11 December 2026.
affiliations_note: Developed with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, which sets its programme, and the newest member of the network with the Guggenheim museums in New York, Venice and Bilbao.

overview: Museum of modern and contemporary art in the cultural district of Saadiyat Island, Abu Dhabi, beside the Louvre Abu Dhabi and the Zayed National Museum (Wikipedia, Hyperallergic).
Abu Dhabi signed the agreement with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation in July 2006. Construction began in 2011, stalled, and the opening slipped from 2013 to 2015, 2017, 2023 and 2025 (Wikipedia).
Named for the Guggenheim Foundation, which runs the programme. Mariët Westermann is director and CEO (Hyperallergic).

Designed by Frank Gehry: 11,600 m² inside with 28 galleries around a central atrium, plus 23,000 m² of outdoor exhibition space across 10 sculptural cones and terraces. Built by BESIX subsidiary Six Construct with Trojan Contracting under a 2021 contract (Khaleej Times, Wikipedia).
The collection covers art from the 1960s to now, with a focus on West Asia, North Africa and South Asia. About 970 works at the start (Khaleej Times, Wikipedia).
Opens on 11 December 2026. General admission Dh70, free for under-18s, UAE students and over-60s (Khaleej Times, 18 September 2026).
details.funding_verdict: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi: Gulf state body: Abu Dhabi government, through its development company and culture department
funding: A 2008 Guggenheim statement said Abu Dhabi's Tourism Development and Investment Company (TDIC) would own the museum and the Foundation would manage its programmes (Wikipedia).
The museum is developed by the Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi, with the Guggenheim Foundation (Khaleej Times).

red_flags.heading: Gulf state body
points: The museum is owned and developed by Abu Dhabi government bodies: the Tourism Development and Investment Company (TDIC) and the Department of Culture and Tourism (Wikipedia; Khaleej Times).

red_flags.heading: Migrant labour abuse on Saadiyat Island
points: Human Rights Watch interviewed 113 Saadiyat workers in 2014 and found steep recruitment fees, withheld wages, passport confiscation, poor housing and deportations after strikes; TDIC's own monitor, PwC, found 88% of 1,050 workers interviewed had paid recruitment fees (Architectural Record, 2015).

HRW did not interview Guggenheim site workers in 2014 because work there was on hold; its researcher said pressure must stay on the project because TDIC, the government developer, runs it (Architectural Record).
TDIC's chief executive Ali Al Hammadi wrote to HRW that workers' rights are "not solely a TDIC challenge alone, but rather an international matter" (Architectural Record).

red_flags.heading: Artist boycott and protests (Gulf Labor Coalition)
points: In March 2011 more than 130 artists and writers pledged not to work with the project until workers' recruitment fees were repaid and an independent monitor published findings (Arab News).
In February 2014 Gulf Labor activists dropped banners including "1% Museum" from the spiral of the Guggenheim in New York (Democracy Now).
In 2015 its offshoot G.U.L.F. occupied the Guggenheim in New York and the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice (Hyperallergic, 2026).
In April 2016 the Guggenheim broke off talks; Richard Armstrong said Gulf Labor kept shifting its demands and spread "mistruths" (Hyperallergic, 2016).
In July 2026 co-founder Andrew Ross said none of the reasons for the action had been adequately resolved (Hyperallergic, 2026).

press.overall: Sustained criticism for about 16 years, almost all about labour conditions and the artist boycott rather than the art programme.

items.title: Anna Lee, "Long-Contested Guggenheim Abu Dhabi Gets Opening Date" (2026)
points: Reports the 11 December opening date after 20 years of delays and 16 years of Gulf Labor's campaign on migrant workers' treatment.
Quotes Ross: "None of the initial reasons for this action have been adequately resolved over the years."
The Guggenheim did not answer a request for comment.

items.title: Hrag Vartanian, "Guggenheim Breaks Off Negotiations with Gulf Labor Over Migrant Rights" (2016)
points: Reports the Guggenheim board's decision of 13 April 2016 to stop negotiating with Gulf Labor, which had asked to meet biweekly to develop the "contractual language needed to build a museum in Abu Dhabi".
Gives Armstrong's answer and Gulf Labor's reply that the museum abandoned good-faith talks.

items.title: Anna Fixsen, "Human Rights Watch Report Documents Continued Migrant Abuse on Saadiyat Island" (2015)
points: Sets out HRW's findings and TDIC's response; notes Gehry worked with a human rights lawyer on safeguards for when construction resumed.

details.bottom_line: The museum is Abu Dhabi state property, with the Guggenheim Foundation running the programme; no fees or costs are published. The weak points are the documented abuse of migrant workers on Saadiyat Island and a boycott that its organisers say was never resolved. Worth watching: whether the Foundation or DCT publishes labour monitoring for the final build.
